title: About training multilingual models
body:
Hi , thanks for your repo! I want to ask some details about training multilingual models. 
1. In your training  stage , did you still follow the rule, the ratio of text batch :speech batch  start with 1:1 and gradually decrease to 0:1 for TTS?   As we all know, for TTS datasets, text and speech should always be one-to-one corresponding, that is, 1:1, 0:1 means there is only speech. Why is the 0:1 situation feasible?

1. 1:1 and 0:1 don't mean text:speech in the way you are thinking. There are 2 datasets one is text:text - i.e. question answer. One if text:speech i.e. a Text prompt and speech response. We only used regular TTS (text followed by speech) sequences for multilingual.
2. Model learns tags very effectively in full parameter finetuning
3. Yes

  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "Orpheus-TTS/orpheus_tts_pypi/orpheus_tts/engine_class.py", line 16, in __init__

title: Is it reasonable to just reverse the order of training data to create a speech-to-text model
body: If I understand everything correctly, is it reasonable and/or a good idea to just reverse the order of the training data? Have the snac tokens be the input and the transcription be the output. Obviously, it would require a retraining of the model but it'd be interesting to see how well the approach would work. In theory, you could use the same pre-tokenized training data.
author: w013nad

comments.body:
This is actually how end-to-end speech models started off - i.e. check out speechgpt - you don't even need to retrain from scratch - you can training using the base model which already has a good correspondence between text and speech and you should get results quickly. You will need to make sure you only calculate the loss on the text tokens if your input_ids look like speech-text otherwise your model will still focus on learning modelling speech tokens using the previous speech tokens. 

You should get okay results - there are models that already work like this - they won't be SOTA like whisper, but from an academic perspective it could be quite interesting,

title: Idea for large scale voice cloning data set with emotion cloning
body:
To build truly high-quality voice acting models, we first need excellent emotion cloning models. A promising approach could be to create a large and diverse audio corpus and extract a speaker embedding for each utterance. Then, we cluster the data by speaker embeddings to create buckets of the same or very similar speakers.

Within each of these speaker-consistent buckets, we perform emotion captioning and then cluster the utterances based on the sentence embeddings of their emotion captions. This gives us smaller buckets that contain utterances with the same speaker and the same emotion—but different textual content.

Once we have the transcriptions of the audio in each of these refined buckets, we can use the utterances as reference and target pairs for training. Pretraining a model on this type of large-scale data, followed by fine-tuning on curated voice acting data from professional studio voice actors, could be a highly effective strategy for building high-quality emotional voice synthesis models.

Just an idea :)
author: christophschuhmann

comments.body: We plan on doing something like this for v1 😊

title: Clarifying Discrepancies in Prompt Construction and Stop Token IDs
body:
Hello, I'd like to ask how exactly the model's prompt is constructed. In orpheus-cpp, the prompt is constructed as:  
```
f"<|audio|>{voice_id}: {text}<|eot_id|><custom_token_4>"
```  
However, in orpheus_tts_pypi the prompt is:  
```
f"<custom_token_3>{voice_id}: {text}<|eot_id|><custom_token_4><custom_token_5><custom_token_1>"
```  
After tokenization, the token IDs are noticeably different. Additionally, the stop token ID for the LLM is unclear: the default is 49158 in orpheus_tts_pypi, and in realtime_streaming_example it is set to 128258. I'm quite confused about this and would appreciate an explanation.
author: HuiResearch

comments.body: Yes same confusionto me also

```def _format_prompt(self, prompt, voice="tara", model_type="larger"):
        if model_type == "smaller":
            if voice:
                return f"<custom_token_3>{prompt}[{voice}]<custom_token_4><custom_token_5>"
            else:
                return f"<custom_token_3>{prompt}<custom_token_4><custom_token_5>"
        else:
            if voice:
                adapted_prompt = f"{voice}: {prompt}"
                prompt_tokens = self.tokeniser(adapted_prompt, return_tensors="pt")
                start_token = torch.tensor([[ 128259]], dtype=torch.int64)
                end_tokens = torch.tensor([[128009, 128260, 128261, 128257]], dtype=torch.int64)
                all_input_ids = torch.cat([start_token, prompt_tokens.input_ids, end_tokens], dim=1)
                prompt_string = self.tokeniser.decode(all_input_ids[0])
                return prompt_string
            else:
                prompt_tokens = self.tokeniser(prompt, return_tensors="pt")
                start_token = torch.tensor([[ 128259]], dtype=torch.int64)
                end_tokens = torch.tensor([[128009, 128260, 128261, 128257]], dtype=torch.int64)
                all_input_ids = torch.cat([start_token, prompt_tokens.input_ids, end_tokens], dim=1)
                prompt_string = self.tokeniser.decode(all_input_ids[0])
                return prompt_string```

ids correlate to custmo_token in the tokenizer.json of the respective model

I think also the tokenizer adds the bos (128000, named SOT in the notebook) before the prompt, so the final structure of a turn looks like:

`SOH 128259 (Start Of Human)` `SOT 128000 (Start Of Text)` `TEXT TOKENS` `EOT 128009 (End Of Text)` `EOH 128260 (End Of Human)` `SOA 128261 (Start Of AI)` `SOS 128257 (Start Of Speech)` `SNAC TOKENS` `EOS 128258 (End Of Speech)` `EOA 128262 (End Of AI)`

so you would end your prompt at SOS and set your end token to EOS to get just the SNAC tokens. And for voice cloning (although it may not work that well), you can make one turn where the text is the transcript, and you pass the encoded voice SNAC tokens, and start another turn with the text you want generated.

None of this is to take for granted, but it seems to work as far as I can tell.

title: Using this for modelling speech-to-speech based models
body:
Hey @amuvarma13 @freddyaboulton @EliasFiz @eltociear @efemaer,

Thanks for open sourcing your work. I was just wondering, how difficult would it be to get it working for speech to speech stuff.
author: thetushargoyal

comments.body:
Depends what you mean for speech to speech. If you mean you talk and it talks back then you can use whisper + LLM + Orpheus to create your system. 

If you mean fully end-to-end speech to speech this model has forgotten a fair amount of text-based reasoning so I wouldn't recommend using it for that task.
let's say want a model that translates or maybe does accent change, can that be directly done in Orpheus? or I need some speech adapter layer?

@amuvarma13 

I was referring to this in your release docs.

> We use the exact same architecture, and training method, to train end-to-end speech models and we'll probably release an open source end-to-end speech model in the coming weeks.

what do end-to-end speech models mean in this context?

Speech in speech out (no separate ASR LLM TTS)- training an LLM on speech tokens to teach it how to speak while also training it on text tokens to maintain its core reasoning capability is the core principle behind most existing multimodal LLMs that do speech today.

Translating is actually a task that I imagine does not require that much text based reasoning so perhaps you could orpheus 3b out of the box - more likely retraining using the pretraining script provided and using text translation qa pairs as the qa dataset is the best solution although this requires a fair amount of compute.

@amuvarma13 do you think training an end to end speech model that translates across languages, hindi speech to english speech with accent preservation might be possible with Orpheus? 

I worked previously on StreamSpeech for direct speech to speech, but that a complicated architecture and requires an additional vocoder and doesn't preserve speaker identity

```
def create_input_ids(example):
    text_ids = tokenizer.encode(example["text"],  add_special_tokens=True)
    text_ids.append(end_of_text)
    example["text_tokens"] = text_ids
    input_ids = (
